drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: An item before anything else. Customer support scenario. Production logs show the agent often calls get customer
drills.answer_line: SAM: But the stem says the descriptions are minimal.
drills.stem: The agent often calls get_customer for order questions instead of lookup_order. Both tools have one-line descriptions and accept similar identifiers. What is the most effective first step to improve tool selection?

options.A: Add 5-8 few-shot examples to the system prompt routing order questions to lookup_order
options.B: Expand each tool's description: input formats, example queries, edge cases, when to use it vs the other
options.C: Add a routing layer that parses each message and pre-selects a tool by keyword
options.D: Merge both into one lookup_entity tool that works out which backend to query

drills.why: Descriptions are minimal, and descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool choice. "First step" rules out merging; routing is over-engineering.

drills.label: Sample question
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Second sample, same scenario. In twelve percent of cases the agent skips get customer
drills.stem: In 12% of cases the agent skips get_customer and calls lookup_order using only the customer's name, occasionally causing the wrong account and an incorrect refund. What change most effectively addresses this?

options.A: A programmatic prerequisite blocking lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns a verified ID
options.B: A system prompt stating verification through get_customer is mandatory before any order operation
options.C: Few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first
options.D: A routing classifier that enables only the tools appropriate to each request type

drills.why: When compliance must be deterministic, prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate. Order that must hold lives in code. D acts on the wrong component.

drills.label: Sample question
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Third sample, Claude Code scenario. You want a slash command called review
drills.answer_line: ALEX: A. "Every developer, clone or pull" means version control
drills.stem: You want a /review slash command that runs the team's checklist, available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository. Where does the file go?

options.A: The .claude/commands folder in the project repository
options.B: The commands folder under .claude in each developer's home directory
options.C: The CLAUDE.md file at the project root
options.D: A .claude/config.json file with a commands array

drills.why: Everyone on the repository means project scope, committed. B is personal scope, C holds instructions not commands, D is an invented file.

drills.question_line: SAM: One more pass before we go. Pause and name the five parts of the game plan
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Sixty items in a hundred and twenty minutes, with the number to select on every item.
drills.prompt: Name the five parts of the game plan: the format, the scenarios, the weights, the pacing, and the method.
drills.answer: 60 items in 120 minutes, number to select on every item. 4 scenarios of 6. Agentic biggest at 27%. Checkpoints at items 20, 40, 60. Four steps, five distractor families.

Pacing with 3 checkpoints and the Review button
A 4-step method for reading any item

The method applied to 3 official sample questions

Both tools: one-line descriptions, similar identifiers
60 items in 120 minutes; pass mark a scaled 720 of 1000

6 scenarios in the bank, 4 drawn per sitting

The four-step method: 1. Constraint words: most effective, first step, NOT, every, money
3. Smallest mechanism that guarantees the outcome
4. Strike out half-right options: one wrong clause and it goes
Distractors: probabilistic fix, over-engineering, wrong layer
Distractors: invented features, scale instead of structure
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: B, expand each tool's description
Tool descriptions are the main mechanism for choosing a tool
Few-shot works around minimal descriptions: a rule carried past its scope
Merging tools is valid but too heavy for a first step
Using the series: Episodes 1 and 10 built on the Foundations score report
Episode 1: the 5 miss patterns; episode 10: zero-score mechanics
Order: 0, 1, then 2-9 by topic, 10, 11 scenarios, 12 exam eve

Recap: the exam tells: If an item says choose two, judge each option alone, like 5 true-or-false questions

If item 20 comes after 37 minutes, or an item passes 2 minutes, answer, flag, move on
If the last line says first step, rule out anything heavier than the cheapest fix
If a prompt instruction guards money or identity, it is a probabilistic fix
If an option names a file or flag you have never seen, treat it as invented
If the tool descriptions are minimal, the fix lives in the descriptions
